generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, being critical is part of how academic work operates. A claim is weighed against the evidence behind it: how it was arrived at, what it rests on, whether others in the field accept it. Across disciplines, a finding is treated not as the last word but as a contribution to an ongoing argument, and being critical means reading your sources the same way.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students given the same source to use in an essay.

Student A reads the source, notes that it supports his point, and quotes its conclusion as evidence. The source has been found and used. But Student A has taken the claim at face value, with no sense of how it was arrived at or whether others in the field read it differently. This is passive reading.

Student B reads the same source and keeps asking questions. What exactly is being claimed? What does it rest on, and how was it tested? Who might disagree? She still uses the source, but now as one voice in a debate, weighed and placed with judgement. This is being critical.

Both students found the same source. Only Student B brought the critical mindset to it, turning a quotation into a judgement.
generatedProse.summary: Being critical is a mindset, not a switch or a fault-finding exercise: it means bringing a questioning, weighing approach to the sources and claims you read. You can now explain what that mindset is and recognise it in how a student approaches a source. The next lessons turn it into practice: engaging with sources actively, and the language that describes critical thinking.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's approach critical rather than passive?

items.text: She questioned the claim, weighed its evidence, and reached a judgement.
She quoted the source's conclusion as evidence for her point.
She read the source more quickly than Student A did.
She accepted the claim because the source was published.

feedback.correct: That's right. Questioning the claim, weighing the evidence and judging it is the critical mindset in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B DID with the source, beyond finding or quoting it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B was critical because she questioned the claim, weighed the evidence and reached a judgement, not because she found or quoted the source faster.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
